b81.content:
A trilogy following the life of a headstrong woman in 14th-century Catholic Norway, from girlhood through a passionate and difficult marriage to old age and a final surrender to God.

Undset became a Catholic in 1924 and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1928, largely for this work.

b82.content:
Chesterton’s lively biography presents Francis as a lover and a "troubadour" of God, and tries to explain to modern readers a saint who seems at once charming and baffling.

It is written with Chesterton’s usual paradox and warmth.

b83.content:
A series of meditations on the person and life of Jesus Christ, drawn from sermons Guardini preached over several years. It walks through the Gospels with both theological depth and reverence.

It became one of the most influential Catholic books of the 20th century.

b84.content:
Chesterton’s portrait of St. Thomas Aquinas, the large, quiet friar nicknamed "the Dumb Ox" by his classmates. It introduces Thomas’s life and his philosophy of common sense and the goodness of created being.

The philosopher Étienne Gilson called it the best book ever written on St. Thomas.

b85.content:
An Australian-born lay apologist and publisher explains the central doctrines of the faith, from the Trinity to the Church, arguing that to see reality as it truly is, one must see it in the light of God.

Its clear style makes it a popular introduction to theology for lay readers.

b86.content:
Tolkien’s epic follows the hobbit Frodo Baggins on a quest to destroy the One Ring. Tolkien, a devout Catholic, described it in a letter as "a fundamentally religious and Catholic work."

Themes of providence, mercy, sacrifice, and humble perseverance run throughout.

b87.content:
A Japanese Catholic novelist tells the story of a 17th-century Portuguese Jesuit who travels to Japan during the persecution of Christians. He struggles with God’s apparent silence in the face of his people’s suffering.

It is a searching, much-debated meditation on faith, weakness, and mercy. Martin Scorsese adapted it for film in 2016.

b88.content:
Paul VI’s encyclical on human life reaffirms Church teaching on marriage and the transmission of life, including its teaching against artificial contraception. It warns of the consequences if sexuality is separated from its meaning.

It was one of the most controversial documents of the modern papacy and remains central to Catholic moral teaching on marriage.

b89.content:
Written as answers to questions from the Italian journalist Vittorio Messori, this book covers topics from the existence of God and the problem of evil to other religions and the meaning of salvation.

It became an international bestseller. The title echoes the words of John Paul II’s first homily as pope: "Be not afraid!"

b90.content:
Benedict XVI’s first encyclical, "God is Love," reflects on the relationship between eros and agape, human and divine love, and on the Church’s charitable work as an essential expression of her nature.

It is known for its warmth and clarity.

b91.content:
An encyclical on Christian hope, taking its title from Romans 8:24, "in hope we were saved." Benedict reflects on the difference between faith-filled hope and modern faith in progress. He draws on the witness of St. Josephine Bakhita and the martyr Paul Le-Bao-Tinh.

It includes a moving reflection on prayer, suffering, and judgment as "settings" for learning hope.

b92.content:
A collection of Mother Teresa’s private letters, published after her death. It revealed that for nearly fifty years she experienced a painful sense of God’s absence, even while serving the poorest of the poor with joy.

It offers a profound witness to faith persevering through spiritual darkness.

b93.content:
Pope Francis’s fourth and final encyclical, on the human and divine love of the Heart of Jesus Christ. It was published during the 350th anniversary of the Sacred Heart apparitions to St. Margaret Mary Alacoque.

It calls a world grown cold and fragmented to rediscover the heart as the center of the person, and Christ’s love as the source of the Church’s mission.

b94.content:
Irenaeus, who as a boy heard St. Polycarp, a disciple of St. John, wrote this five-book work to refute the Gnostic sects that claimed a secret knowledge hidden from ordinary Christians.

Against them he set the public teaching handed down from the apostles through the succession of bishops, especially in the church of Rome. It is one of the earliest witnesses to the canon of the four Gospels and to the idea of apostolic tradition.

b95.content:
Addressed to the Emperor Antoninus Pius, Justin’s Apology defends Christians against the charges of atheism and immorality and presents the faith as the fulfillment of both philosophy and the Hebrew prophets.

Its closing chapters give the oldest detailed description of Christian worship: the Sunday gathering, the readings from the apostles and prophets, the homily, and the Eucharist, which Justin says is the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus.

b96.content:
When the church of Corinth deposed its presbyters, the church of Rome wrote to restore peace. Tradition attributes the letter to Clement, an early bishop of Rome.

It urges humility, repentance, and good order, drawing examples from the Old Testament and from the martyrdoms of Peter and Paul. It was read aloud in some churches alongside Scripture and is one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament.

b97.content:
Basil wrote this treatise to defend the full divinity of the Holy Spirit against those who denied that the Spirit should be worshiped with the Father and the Son.

He argues from Scripture, from the Church’s baptismal formula, and from the unwritten traditions of the liturgy. The work prepared the way for the Council of Constantinople in 381, which added to the Creed that the Spirit is "worshiped and glorified" with the Father and the Son.

b98.content:
Written as a dialogue between John and his friend Basil, whom he had tricked into accepting ordination while avoiding it himself, this treatise explains why John felt unworthy of so great an office.

It describes the dignity and dangers of the priesthood, the virtues a pastor needs, and the power of preaching, and has been read by priests and seminarians for sixteen centuries.

b99.content:
Also known by its Latin title De Doctrina Christiana, this handbook teaches how to understand and explain the Scriptures. Augustine discusses signs and things, the rule of love as the key to interpretation, and how to read difficult passages.

The final book, on Christian preaching, adapted classical rhetoric for the service of the Gospel. The work shaped Christian education throughout the Middle Ages.

b100.content:
Written soon after Gregory became pope, this guide for bishops and pastors explains who should take up the care of souls, how they should live, and how to teach different kinds of people, from the rich and poor to the proud and the timid.

It became the standard handbook for bishops in the medieval West and was translated into Old English by King Alfred the Great.

b101.content:
In conversation with his deacon Peter, Gregory tells the stories of the holy men and women of Italy, their miracles and their deaths. The second of its four books is the only early life of St. Benedict of Nursia.

The Dialogues were among the most widely read books of the Middle Ages and shaped how Christians imagined holiness, miracles, and the life to come.

b102.content:
In this dialogue with his pupil Boso, Anselm asks why God had to become man to save the world. His answer, that only one who is both God and man could make satisfaction for humanity’s sin against the infinite honor of God, became one of the most influential theories of the Atonement.

The book is a model of "faith seeking understanding," showing reason at work on the mysteries of faith.

b103.content:
Scivias, short for "Know the Ways of the Lord," records twenty-six visions Hildegard received and the explanations given to her, covering creation, the Fall, redemption, the Church, and the end of time.

The manuscript was illuminated with striking images of her visions. Pope Eugene III read portions of it and encouraged her to continue writing.

b104.content:
Aquinas wrote this work, traditionally at the request of St. Raymond of Penyafort, to present the Christian faith to those who do not accept the authority of Scripture, such as Muslim and Jewish thinkers.

The first three books use reason alone to show God’s existence, nature, and providence; the fourth turns to truths known only by revelation, such as the Trinity, the Incarnation, and the sacraments.

b105.content:
Commissioned by the Franciscan order, Bonaventure’s life of St. Francis became the official biography for centuries. It traces Francis’s conversion, his love of poverty, the founding of the order, and the stigmata at La Verna.

Bonaventure presents Francis as a mirror of Christ and as a guide in the soul’s ascent to God. Giotto’s famous frescoes in Assisi follow its account.

b106.content:
Catherine was a married laywoman in Genoa who worked for decades in the city’s hospital. Her short treatise describes purgatory from within, as a fire of God’s love that purifies the soul.

The souls there, she writes, suffer greatly, yet are filled with a joy surpassed only by that of heaven, because they desire nothing but to be made fit for God.

b107.content:
Louis of Granada was a Spanish Dominican and one of the great spiritual writers of the 16th century. The Sinner’s Guide offers the reasons why we should love and serve God, and a practical path out of sin into a life of virtue.

St. Teresa of Ávila, St. Francis de Sales, and St. Charles Borromeo all recommended it.

b108.content:
John began this poem while imprisoned in a tiny cell in Toledo. Inspired by the Song of Songs, it tells of a bride searching for her Beloved through the mountains and meadows until she is united with him.

John later wrote a long commentary explaining each stanza as a stage in the soul’s journey to spiritual marriage with Christ. It is among the greatest poems in the Spanish language.

b109.content:
In four short stanzas and a commentary, John describes the highest state of union with God possible in this life, in which the Holy Spirit burns in the soul like a gentle, living flame.

Written for a laywoman, Doña Ana de Peñalosa, it is the most joyful of John’s works, describing not the dark night but the dawn of love that follows it.

b110.content:
Written during a retreat late in Bellarmine’s life, this little book climbs fifteen "steps" from the visible world to its Creator, considering the earth, the waters, the heavens, the human soul, and the angels.

Each step leads the reader from the beauty and order of creation to the perfections of God and to the love He deserves.

b111.content:
As a young priest in the Chablais region of Savoy, which had become Calvinist, Francis wrote leaflets explaining the Catholic faith and slipped them under doors when people refused to hear him preach.

Collected and published after his death, they patiently defend the authority of the Church, Scripture and Tradition, and the sacraments. His gentleness helped win back much of the region to the Church.

b112.content:
This small book offers thirty-one short meditations, one for each day of the month, to accompany a visit to Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament, along with prayers of spiritual communion and visits to Our Lady.

It was one of the most popular devotional books of the 18th and 19th centuries and helped spread the practice of Eucharistic adoration.

b113.content:
Alphonsus considered this his most useful work. Built around St. Paul’s hymn to love in 1 Corinthians 13, it shows how each quality of charity, from patience and kindness to humility and perseverance, is practiced in daily life.

Its message is simple: all holiness consists in loving Jesus Christ.

b114.content:
Newman’s most philosophical work asks how ordinary people can rightly be certain of things they cannot strictly prove, including the truths of religion.

He distinguishes notional from real assent and describes the "illative sense," the mind’s ability to weigh many converging probabilities and reach a firm conclusion. It remains a classic of the philosophy of religious belief.

b115.content:
Commissioned by the bishops of the United States, the Baltimore Catechism taught the faith to generations of American Catholics in short questions and answers to be memorized, such as "Who made us? God made us."

It was the standard Catholic school textbook in the United States from the 1880s until the 1960s and is still used by many families today.

b116.content:
Leo XIII’s encyclical on Christian philosophy called for the restoration of the philosophy of St. Thomas Aquinas in Catholic schools and seminaries.

It argues that faith and reason, rightly understood, never contradict each other, and that sound philosophy prepares the way for faith. It sparked a great revival of Thomistic thought in the late 19th and 20th centuries.

b117.content:
Written forty years after Rerum Novarum, in the depths of the Great Depression, this encyclical on the reconstruction of the social order criticizes both unrestrained capitalism and communism.

It is famous for formulating the principle of subsidiarity: that larger bodies should not take over what smaller communities, such as families and local associations, can do for themselves.

b118.content:
Issued in the middle of the Second World War, this encyclical teaches that the Church is the Mystical Body of Christ, with Christ as its Head and the Holy Spirit as its soul.

It explains how the members of the Church are united to Christ and to one another, and calls the faithful to love the Church as Christ’s own Body. Its themes were taken up by the Second Vatican Council.

b119.content:
In this apostolic exhortation on evangelization in the modern world, Paul VI declares that the Church "exists in order to evangelize."

He emphasizes the witness of life, the explicit proclamation of Jesus, and the evangelization of cultures, and observes that people today listen more willingly to witnesses than to teachers. It inspired the "New Evangelization" of later popes.

b120.content:
John Paul II’s first encyclical, "The Redeemer of Man," sets out the vision of his whole pontificate: that Christ reveals man to himself and that the human person is the way of the Church.

It defends human dignity and freedom against the threats of a technological age, and was read in Communist Poland and beyond as a charter of human rights rooted in the Gospel.
